successor: Clusium under Lars Porsenna (brief occupation), then Early Roman Republic
source1: Gary E. Forsythe, 'Ancient Rome: Early centuries of the Roman Republic', Encyclopaedia Britannica - https://www.britannica.com/place/ancient-Rome/Early-centuries-of-the-Roman-Republic
source2: Ronald T. Ridley, 'The Puzzles of Porsenna', Studi Etruschi 78 - https://www.studietruschi.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/SE78_07.pdf
notes: Tradition: aristocrats expelled Tarquin c.509 (EBSCO/Phillips). Britannica's prevalent modern view and Ridley (citing Tacitus): Porsenna of Clusium seized or received Rome's surrender within W, so priority rule gives T2. Sources disagree; dates legendary.

successor: Hallstatt A-B1 (Late Bronze Age, Paris Basin)
source1: Samantha Brunel et al., 'Ancient genomes from present-day France unveil 7,000 years of its demographic history', PNAS 117(23), 2020 - https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7293694
notes: No recorded central authority. Brunel et al. find genetic continuity from Bronze to Iron Age France, transition mainly by cultural diffusion; Britannica says Urnfield spread perhaps tied to folk migrations. Paris Basin samples not specified; inference only.

successor: British New Guinea (Papua from 1906), colonial administration
source1: Christopher S. Latham, 'Orokaiva', Encyclopedia of World Cultures (via Encyclopedia.com) - https://www.encyclopedia.com/humanities/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/orokaiva
source2: William Standish, 'Papua New Guinea: The colonial period', Encyclopaedia Britannica - https://www.britannica.com/place/Papua-New-Guinea/The-colonial-period
notes: Acephalous society, no central authority. Protectorate 1884, annexation 1888; gold miners entered Northern District amid killings on both sides; colonial rule via appointed village constables. Effective control postdates DB 1883; Q3 Y denotes lost autonomy.

successor: Kalmar Union (Norway as a kingdom under union monarch Erik of Pomerania)
source2: Helge Salvesen, Per G. Norseng, Erik Opsahl, Ida Scott, 'Kalmarunionen', Store norske leksikon, 2024 - https://snl.no/Kalmarunionen
notes: Dynastic union: Olav ruled Norway and Denmark, Margrete succeeded, Erik acclaimed king of Norway 1389, crowned at Kalmar 1397. Shared monarch and foreign policy; each realm kept its laws and council, so Norwegian authority persisted. No conquest.

successor: Classical Angkor (Khmer Empire under the Mahidharapura dynasty)
notes: 1100 is a period break. A new dynasty began ruling at Angkor in the late 11th century; Suryavarman II defeated rival claimants, reuniting the empire after over 50 years of unrest (Q4). Angkorian state apparatus continued.

source1: Michael Vickery, 'Funan Reviewed: Deconstructing the Ancients', Bulletin de l'Ecole francaise d'Extreme-Orient 90-91, 2003 - http://michaelvickery.org/vickery2003funan.pdf
source2: Britannica Editors (rev. Virginia Gorlinski), 'Funan', Encyclopaedia Britannica - https://www.britannica.com/place/Funan
notes: Standard (Coedes) account: Funan overthrown by its vassal Chenla, late 6th or early 7th century, internal under vassal rule. Britannica: incorporated into Chenla in 6th century. Vickery notes ruling-class continuity and doubts conquest; dates uncertain.

successor: Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth (occupation of Moscow 1610-1612), then Romanov Tsardom of Russia (1613)
source1: Chester Dunning, 'Time of Troubles', Encyclopedia of Russian History (via Encyclopedia.com) - https://www.encyclopedia.com/history/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/time-troubles
source2: Andrew B. Wachtel et al., 'Russia: The Time of Troubles', Encyclopaedia Britannica - https://www.britannica.com/place/Russia/The-Time-of-Troubles
notes: After civil war and pretenders, Shuisky deposed 1610; boyars invited Wladyslaw, Poles imposed a military dictatorship in Moscow until expelled October 1612 (priority rule: T2). Romanov elected 1613; institutions largely restored, so T0 reading possible.

source1: Samantha Brunel et al., 'Ancient genomes from present-day France unveil 7,000 years of its demographic history', PNAS 117(23), 2020 - https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7293694
source2: Britannica Editors, 'La Tene', Encyclopaedia Britannica - https://www.britannica.com/topic/La-Tene
notes: Typological sub-phase of a continuous La Tene sequence, no recorded central authority. Brunel et al.: Hallstatt and La Tene individuals in France show similar affinities, genetic continuity. Britannica links La Tene B to Celtic migrations; Paris Basin specifics not shown.

source1: M. Joseph Costelloe and Thomas H. Watkins, 'Augustan Settlement', EBSCO Research Starters, 2022 - https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/augustan-settlement
source2: Britannica Editors, 'Why did the Roman Republic end?', Encyclopaedia Britannica - https://www.britannica.com/question/Why-did-the-Roman-Republic-end
notes: Insider Octavian won the civil wars at Actium (31 BCE), seized control and became autocratic ruler; the 27 BCE settlement created a new form of government, the principate, keeping republican forms. No external conquest; civil wars precede (Q4).

source2: Prosopography of the Byzantine Empire (King's College London), 'Katakylas 1' - https://pbe.kcl.ac.uk/data/D42/F60.htm
notes: Basil I, co-emperor from 866, murdered Michael III in 867 and founded the Macedonian dynasty; same imperial apparatus at Constantinople. Thomas the Slav's rebellion (821-823) besieged Constantinople (Q4). Crete lost to Arabs, outside core.
